1079.title: Parvati's tapas
1079.hook: a young ascetic visits Parvati in the forest and mocks the god she loves, and she won't stay to listen
1079.carry: parvati won shiva by tapas, not looks
1079.howItsDone: Parvati's austerity to win Shiva is remembered in festivals such as Hartalika Teej, when some Hindu women fast and pray in her honor, and her story is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week of Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and Saraswati, ending with Saraswati as the speech in a giant's mouth. Today, the last of the five.

A princess has left her father's palace in the Himalayas for the forest. She tried to win the great ascetic Shiva the ordinary way: beauty, flowers, the god of love himself taking aim at Shiva. It went badly. Shiva opened his third eye, burned the god of love to ash, and walked away. So the princess changes her plan. If Shiva lives by austerity, she will out-austere him. In Kalidasa's poem, The Birth of Kumara, that's where we find her: alone in the forest, taking up the life of an ascetic. Today, Parvati.
screen: `A PRINCESS LEAVES THE PALACE.` → `LOVE IS BURNED TO ASH.` → `SHE CHANGES HER PLAN.`

segments.voice: Kalidasa describes her austerity season by season: standing among fires in the summer heat, in cold water through winter nights, living on less and less, until she gives up eating even fallen leaves. That, the poem says, is why those who know the old stories call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf. One day a visitor comes: a young ascetic with matted hair. He asks why someone so lovely is doing all this. When he learns it's for Shiva, he starts, very gently, to make fun of her choice. Shiva? Who wears snakes and ash, rides an old bull, haunts cremation grounds? Nobody even knows his family. A princess like you, with him? Parvati doesn't laugh along, and she doesn't crumble. She defends Shiva point by point, then does something sharper. She tells her companion to stop him, because whoever speaks badly of a great soul does wrong, and so does whoever stays and listens. And she turns to walk away. Then the young ascetic drops the disguise. He was Shiva all along, testing her. In the poem he says that from now on he's hers, won by her austerity. This is tapas, one of Hinduism's big words: heat, the fire of discipline, austerity offered up. Parvati's tapas isn't punishment; it's devotion that won't quit. Beauty failed. Steady devotion won the lord of yogis. And it's why, in parts of India, women keep the Hartalika Teej fast in her name, many going without food and even water for the day, praying as she did.
screen: `AUSTERITY, SEASON BY SEASON.` · `APARNA: NOT EVEN A LEAF.` · `A VISITOR MOCKS HER CHOICE.` · `IT WAS SHIVA ALL ALONG.` · then, large: `TAPAS: DEVOTION THAT WON'T QUIT.`

segments.voice: Hindus keep tapas in small, everyday forms: a vrat, a vow, like a fast on a set day of the week, or a mantra said every morning no matter what. Choose one small vow for this week. If you pray, offer it to Parvati or God; if you don't, keep it steady anyway, as Parvati did.
Durga. The name over these five; and some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods: the patient one in the forest, the warrior on the lion. Today's word.
Your line: Parvati won Shiva by tapas, not looks. Tomorrow, Parvati and an empty kitchen. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1080.title: Annapurna's open kitchen
1080.hook: Shiva calls the world an illusion, food and all, so Parvati vanishes, and the kitchens of the world go empty
1080.carry: food is the goddess's gift, so offer it first
1080.howItsDone: Annapurna is honored in homes and kitchens as the goddess of nourishment, and her temple in Varanasi stands near the Kashi Vishwanath temple of Shiva; some families offer a little food to her before a meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parvati won Shiva by tapas, not looks: she outlasted him at austerity and turned her back on his mockery, until he dropped the disguise.

On Kailash, an argument. Shiva, the great ascetic, is explaining that the world of things is illusion, maya: bodies, houses, possessions, even food, none of it ultimately real. Parvati listens. Then, in the story people tell, she decides to let him find out what that means. She disappears, and with her goes every grain, every loaf, every pot on every stove. The fields stand empty. Creatures go hungry. Even the gods grow faint. Even Shiva. Today, Parvati again, and an argument made without a single word.
screen: `SHIVA: EVEN FOOD IS ILLUSION.` → `PARVATI DISAPPEARS.` → `EVERY KITCHEN GOES EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Word comes that somewhere food is still being served. In Kashi, the holy city of Varanasi, a kitchen is open, and at its door stands a goddess with a ladle and a pot that never runs out, feeding everyone who comes. Her name in this story is Annapurna, which tradition explains as the one who is full of food. So Shiva, lord of the universe, the great ascetic who said food was unreal, walks to Kashi with a begging bowl and holds it out to her. And she fills it. The images of this moment are tender, not triumphant: the goddess serving, the god receiving, a family meal. Some tellers say Shiva learned that the body and its hunger aren't to be waved away. Some say Parvati wasn't arguing against his teaching at all, but filling it out: in that reading, spirit needs a body to live in, and a body needs to eat. In Varanasi a temple to Annapurna stands near Shiva's own, and devotees speak of her as the mother who makes sure no one in the city goes hungry. This is why many Hindu homes treat food as holy. Before eating, a family offers it first, to Annapurna, to Krishna, to the home's deity, and what comes back is prasad, a gift returned. The old teaching goes deep: in the Taittiriya Upanishad, the seeker Bhrigu's first discovery is that food is Brahman. And with that the five goddesses are met. Tomorrow, the one power moving through them all.

segments.voice: Before your next meal, do what many Hindu families do: set a little aside first, or hold the plate still a moment, and offer it. Trace it back while you wait: who cooked it, who carried it, who grew it, the rain, the soil. Then eat it as a gift returned. If you pray, offer it to Annapurna or God in your own words; if you don't, thank the hands.
Durga. The name over all five goddesses met in this run; today, the Goddess as Annapurna, filling Shiva's bowl. Today's word.

1081.title: Ramakrishna's snake
1081.hook: a snake lying coiled and a snake on the move: is it one snake or two?
1081.carry: shakti is the one reality in motion
1081.howItsDone: In Shakta traditions the Goddess is worshipped as the supreme reality, and some teachers in Ramakrishna's line still explain Brahman and Shakti with his images of fire and its burning, and the snake at rest and moving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food is the goddess's gift: Annapurna filled Shiva's bowl, and the run of five goddesses closed. Today, from five stories to one idea.

A snake lies coiled on a warm rock, perfectly still. Then, without warning, it uncoils and glides off into the grass. Is the still snake one thing and the moving snake another? Obviously not. It's the same snake, resting, then acting. Ramakrishna, the Kali priest this path met last week, is remembered using that plain picture to answer an old question, the question at the heart of today: what is Shakti?
screen: `A SNAKE, COILED AND STILL.` → `THE SAME SNAKE, MOVING.` → `ONE SNAKE, OR TWO?`

segments.voice: Shakti is Sanskrit for power, energy, the ability to act. In the stories, a god has a shakti, a power often pictured as a goddess at his side. But in the Shakta traditions, which hold the Goddess as the highest reality, that picture turns over. Shakti isn't a power that someone else owns. She is the one. The path watched this in the Devi Mahatmya, when she drew every goddess on the battlefield back into herself. Now the old question. Hindu philosophy also speaks of Brahman, the absolute, beyond change and action. Is the still absolute one thing and the active Goddess another? The stories told by Ramakrishna's followers say he answered with pictures. Fire and its power to burn: you can't have one without the other. Milk and its whiteness. A gem and its shine. And the snake. When the absolute is thought of at rest, he called it Brahman. When it creates, sustains and dissolves the world, he called it Shakti, or Kali, or Mother. One reality, resting or moving. If the moving world is Shakti, it isn't a distraction from the holy. The cooking, the traffic, the growing, the grieving: in Shakta thought, that's the Goddess at work. Teachers in different schools put this differently. Some describe the changing world as maya, a kind of appearance; Shakta teachers tend to speak of it as her play. This path holds both up and ranks neither. For those who think the Shakta way, it's like the fire: you don't have to look past the heat to find the flame.
screen: `SHAKTI: POWER, THE ABILITY TO ACT.` · `NOT A POWER OWNED, BUT THE ONE.` · `FIRE AND ITS POWER TO BURN.` · `THE MOVING WORLD AS HER PLAY.` · then, large: `ONE REALITY, RESTING OR MOVING.`

segments.voice: Look at a diya, a candle or a lamp if one is near, or bring a flame to mind, and notice that you can't pull the light apart from the warmth. Then turn to your own body, the quiet awareness simply here and the breath moving through it, and rest in both at once without separating them. If you pray, hold the name Shakti, or Ma, gently; if you don't, stay with the flame.
Shakti as a philosophy. Power, energy, the ability to act, which Shakta traditions hold to be the Goddess herself, one with the absolute, the way fire is one with its burning. Today's word.
Your line: Shakti is the one reality in motion. Tomorrow, one verse about Shiva and Shakti. See you tomorrow.

1082.title: Shiva cannot stir
1082.hook: a long hymn to the goddess opens with a sentence about a god who cannot even stir
1082.howItsDone: The Saundarya Lahari is chanted and studied by worshippers of the goddess, including in the Shri Vidya tradition, and a reading of it begins with this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti is the one reality in motion, like Ramakrishna's snake, coiled or gliding. Today, one verse puts it in Shiva's terms.

A long Sanskrit hymn to the goddess, the Saundarya Lahari, the wave of beauty, opens in a strange place. Not with her face, her weapons or her lion. It begins with Shiva, the great god of the mountain, the destroyer, the lord of yogis. And what stands out in that first verse is what he can't do. Without her, the verse says, he can't create. He can't even stir. Tradition says the hymn comes from Shankara, the teacher of non-duality. Whoever wrote it chose to open a praise of the goddess with God standing perfectly still.
screen: `THE WAVE OF BEAUTY.` → `IT OPENS WITH SHIVA.` → `WITHOUT HER, HE CAN'T STIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create. If not, this god is not even able to move. So how could anyone without merit bow to you, or praise you, you who are worshipped by Vishnu, by Shiva, by Brahma? First, the play on words in the Sanskrit. Joined with shakti, power, the word this path first met in Durga's story, Shiva becomes shakta, able. The verse sets the two sounds side by side, and the second time the sound means capable. Second, the couple. In the Puranas, Shiva and Parvati are married, with children. The verse doesn't deny that. But it says something sharper. She isn't only his wife. She is the reason anything he does gets done. Stillness on one side, movement on the other, and nothing happens until the two are together. Third, the ending. Vishnu who protects, Brahma who creates, Shiva who dissolves: in this hymn, all of them stand before her. Some who worship the goddess hear that line as the whole point. In their reading, power isn't a tool God picks up. It's the face of God that acts. And a fourth, closer to home. You can hear this teaching in how Hindus name the divine couples: Sita-Ram, Radhe-Shyam, Gauri-Shankar, the goddess first. Many teachers explain it this way: you come to God through his Shakti. And in a Shiva temple, the linga rises from a base many read as Shakti, the two worshipped together.
screen: `JOINED WITH SHAKTI, SHIVA IS ABLE.` · `SHAKTI AND SHAKTA: POWER AND ABLE.` · `THE GODS THEMSELVES BOW TO HER.` · `SITA-RAM, RADHE-SHYAM, GAURI-SHANKAR.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HER, HE CANNOT EVEN STIR.`

segments.voice: If there's a picture of Shiva and Parvati near you, or of any divine couple, look at it a while: the still one and the one who moves. Then say a pair's name slowly, the goddess first, the way Hindu families do: Gauri-Shankar, Sita-Ram, Radhe-Shyam. If you pray, let the names be your prayer, one with each breath out. If you don't, notice the stillness in you, and the breath that moves it.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the wave of beauty's opening verse, Shiva joined with Shakti is able to create. Without her, he cannot even stir.
Your line: Shiva cannot stir without Shakti. That's why her name so often comes first. Until tomorrow.

1083.title: The blade of grass
1083.hook: a single blade of grass that fire cannot burn and wind cannot lift
1083.carry: every power is borrowed from brahman
1083.howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Vedanta schools, and the scene of Uma explaining Brahman to Indra is retold in talks on the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva cannot stir without Shakti: the wave of beauty's first verse, and the goddess's name first.

The gods have just won a victory, and they're very pleased with themselves. So begins a short scene in the Kena Upanishad. Then something appears that they don't recognize: a mysterious being, a yaksha. Agni, the fire, goes up to it, boasting that he can burn anything on earth. The being sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. Agni throws everything he has at it. The grass doesn't even scorch. Then Vayu, the wind, who says he can carry off anything at all. He can't lift it an inch. Two gods, two powers, one straw.
screen: `THE GODS ARE PROUD.` → `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `FIRE CAN'T BURN IT. WIND CAN'T LIFT IT.`

segments.voice: Next the gods send Indra, their king. He walks toward the being, and it vanishes. In that same space he meets a woman, radiant and beautifully adorned: Uma, the daughter of the Himalaya. He asks what it was. She answers: that was Brahman, the ultimate reality. Your victory was its victory, and you took the credit. First, the lesson about power. Fire could burn and wind could blow because something greater let them. Take that away, and even a blade of grass is too heavy. The gods' powers were real, but borrowed. Second, who explains it. The one who can name Brahman to the king of the gods is Uma, a woman of the mountains. Later tradition knows Uma as a name of Parvati, Shiva's wife. Some who worship the goddess point to this scene: when the gods are lost, Shakti is the teacher who stands in the empty place and speaks. Third, where she appears: in the very space where the being vanished. Some readers hear the heart of the idea there. Brahman is beyond sight, beyond fire and wind; Shakti is the side of that reality that turns toward you, the face that answers. Fourth, the plainest. The scene begins with pride, the ego, ahankara, saying I did this, and ends with a question. That's why so many Hindus close a prayer or a day's work by offering it back: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna. The Upanishad says Agni, Vayu and Indra came to stand above the other gods because they came closest to Brahman, and Indra above them because he was the first to know it.
screen: `THE GODS' POWERS WERE BORROWED.` · `THE BEING VANISHES. UMA IS THERE.` · `UMA IS THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · `PRIDE SAYS: I DID THIS.` · then, large: `THAT WAS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that went well this week. Trace the power behind it: the breath, the teachers, the body you didn't make. Then do what many Hindus do at the end of a prayer or a task, and offer it back. If you pray, say Krishnarpanam, or offered to you, in the name you use for God. If you don't, say quietly: not only mine.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Kena Upanishad, fire and wind fail before one blade of grass, and Uma stands where the mystery vanished and names it Brahman.
Your line: every power is borrowed from Brahman. Even fire burns only because Brahman lets it. See you tomorrow.

1084.title: The hidden power
1084.hook: sages ask what caused the world, then sit down to meditate, and see a power hidden in plain sight
1084.carry: god's power hides in the world; stillness sees it
1084.howItsDone: The Shvetashvatara Upanishad is read and chanted in Vedanta and Shaiva study, and its verse on God's hidden power is quoted by teachers explaining the idea of shakti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every power is borrowed from Brahman: fire couldn't burn a blade of grass, wind couldn't lift it, and Uma named the power behind them.

What is the cause? Where did we come from? By what do we live? Where do we rest? Those are the questions that open the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. A group of seekers run through the usual answers: time, nature, chance, the elements. None of them settles it. So they turn from the list. They sit, and they meditate. And the next verse says what they saw. Not a new theory. A power, hidden. Today the word shakti steps out of the stories and into an Upanishad.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CAUSE?` → `THE USUAL ANSWERS DON'T SETTLE IT.` → `THEY STOP TALKING, AND SIT.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Those who followed the path of meditation saw the power of God's own self, hidden in its own qualities. The Sanskrit is devatma shakti: the shakti of the divine self. Notice three things. First, it's seen in meditation, not argued into. The list ran out, they sat, and then they saw. Second, the power is hidden in a surprising place: in its own qualities. The power behind the world is covered by the world it makes, the way a person can be hidden by their own good work. You see the painting and forget the painter's hand. Third, the power belongs to God's own self. It isn't a second thing standing beside God. Later the same Upanishad comes back to it. His highest power, the text says, is heard of as many-sided, and his knowledge, strength and action belong to his nature. Knowing, strength, doing: shakti is the name for God in action. One more line draws the map. Know that maya is prakriti, nature, and that the great Lord is the one who wields maya. Teachers read the word maya there in more than one way, but the shape of the verse is plain: the power that makes nature is in the Lord's hand. In this Upanishad, the power that makes the world is God's own, folded so deeply into what we see that it takes stillness to notice it. That's why dhyana, meditation, sits beside prayer in Hindu practice: not to invent the divine, but to see it.
screen: `THE SEEKERS SIT AND MEDITATE.` · `GOD'S OWN POWER, HIDDEN IN ITS QUALITIES.` · `KNOWING, STRENGTH, DOING.` · `DHYANA: NOT INVENTING, SEEING.` · then, large: `DEVATMA SHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus sit each morning, before the day's noise, in dhyana. Sit now and look at one ordinary thing near you: a plant, your hand, the light on a wall. Don't explain it. Let the answers pass, the way the seekers let their list go, and keep looking for the power hidden in it. If you pray, rest in the name you use for God; if you don't, rest in the looking.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, seekers in meditation see God's own power, hidden in its own qualities.
Your line: God's power hides in the world, and stillness sees it. You see the painting; the painter's hand is in it. Same time tomorrow.

1085.title: Krishna's two natures
1085.hook: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, the sense of I: in the Gita, Krishna calls the whole list his nature, and then says there's more
1085.carry: even the mind is prakriti, god's nature
1085.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita's seventh chapter is studied and chanted in homes and Gita classes, and teachers use its two natures, lower and higher, to explain how the divine relates to the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God's power hides in the world: seekers set down their list of answers, sat, and saw it hidden in its own qualities.

Earth. Water. Fire. Air. Space. Mind. Intellect. The sense of I. In the seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists these one after another, the way you'd unpack a box onto a table. The ground under your feet, the thoughts in your head, even the feeling of being someone: all on one list. Then he says: this is my nature. Mine. And before Arjuna can take that in, he adds: and this is the lower one. There's another.
screen: `EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR, SPACE.` → `MIND, INTELLECT, THE SENSE OF I.` → `THIS IS MY NATURE. THE LOWER ONE.`

segments.voice: Here are the verses, in paraphrase. Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of I: this is my prakriti, my nature, divided eightfold. That is the lower. Know my other, higher nature, the life in things, by which this whole world is upheld. All beings come from these two, as from a womb. I am where the whole world begins, and where it dissolves. First, the word. Prakriti: nature, the stuff and the shaping of things. Krishna calls it his. Matter isn't the enemy of the divine here; it belongs to God. Second, what's on the lower list. Mind, intellect and the sense of I are there too. The thoughts you're thinking right now are, in the Gita's picture, part of nature, moving like weather. Many teachers draw the lesson plainly: your racing thoughts are prakriti at work, not the deepest you. Third, the higher nature: the life that holds the world up. Some readers hear every living being in it; others hear the spark of awareness in each one. Either way, the world doesn't just sit there. It's held. Fourth, the week. Here the Gita speaks through Krishna; in the days ahead, a goddess text takes up this same word, prakriti, in her own voice. Look back. Parvati's tapas, and her kitchen in Kashi. Ramakrishna's snake. Shiva who can't stir without Shakti. A blade of grass, and Uma who named the power behind it. Seekers who saw God's power hidden in the world. And now Krishna: all of this is mine, and there is more.
screen: `PRAKRITI: MY NATURE, EIGHTFOLD.` · `EVEN MIND AND THE SENSE OF I.` · `THE HIGHER NATURE HOLDS THE WORLD UP.` · `THE WEEK: A VERSE, A STRAW, A SEEING.` · then, large: `ALL OF THIS IS MINE, AND THERE IS MORE.`

segments.voice: Walk Krishna's list slowly, one breath each: earth, your weight on the seat; water, the wet of the mouth; fire, warm hands; air, the breath; space, the room; mind, the next thought; intellect, the part that names it; the sense of I. Then rest in whatever is aware of the whole list. If you pray, you can offer the list back in the words you use.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Gita, earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of I make up the lower nature, and a higher one holds the world up.
Your line: even the mind is prakriti, God's nature. A racing mind is nature moving. Rest well.
